headlines.title: Wall Street's AI Debt Machine Is Starting to Choke on Supply
headlines.summary: This newspaper has long argued that the credit market, not the equity market, is where AI euphoria will first encounter its reckoning — and here, precisely, is the evidence. Early signs that debt markets are approaching absorption limits for AI infrastructure financing threatens the capital pipeline underpinning hyperscaler capex, with direct read-through to Nvidia, the broader semiconductor complex, and the investment-grade credit spreads that have thus far remained implausibly serene. On a day when Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close and the Federal Reserve deliberates on rates, a structural warning from the credit side of the ledger is the most consequential piece of analysis in the room.

headlines.title: SK Hynix delivered on third-quarter results — but the outlook is what really mattered to Wall Street and the AI trade
headlines.summary: SK Hynix's declaration that HBM supply constraints will persist through 2030 is, for the AI trade, rather more than a quarterly earnings footnote — it is a forward guidance statement of the first order, one that simultaneously validates Nvidia's pricing power and raises uncomfortable questions about the pace at which AI infrastructure can actually be assembled. The 11% surge in Hynix shares has already propagated through Samsung, the Nikkei, and the KOSPI; one may reasonably expect the reverberations to reach Micron and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index when New York opens in earnest.

headlines.title: Oil up over 1% as Saudi Arabian refinery attack reignites supply risk concerns
headlines.summary: A Houthi missile strike on the Ras Tanura refinery — one of the world's largest crude processing facilities — is precisely the sort of kinetic event that transforms geopolitical background noise into an immediate supply-risk premium. With Brent already elevated and Saudi exports running near wartime highs, any disruption to refinery throughput tightens the product market rather than merely the crude one, with disproportionate consequences for diesel and jet fuel. Energy equities, airline cost structures, and the broader inflation outlook all feel the draught simultaneously, arriving at a peculiarly inconvenient moment for a Federal Reserve already navigating persistently elevated price pressures.
